Reflections on Sefer Devarim

From Self to Surrender: A Journey Through Elul and Tishrei

By Rabbi Binyamin Goldberg

Volume I: Sefer Devarim

Diburim (דִּבּוּרִים) — "Spoken Words"

This series captures divrei Torah originally spoken and recorded, then transcribed and refined into written form.

TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chapter 1 — Parashat Devarim: Not Just Their Story, Ours Too

Chapter 4 — Parashat Re'eh: Bracha, Avodah Zarah, and Tzedakah as One Path

INTRODUCTION

Why I wrote this

Over the last several months, I’ve had the opportunity to work on a series of Divrei Torah that eventually came together into this Kuntres, now called Diburim — reflections based on Sefer Devarim. The name Diburim holds a dual meaning. It echoes Sefer Devarim—the Book of “Words”—and also the living “speech” through which these Torah thoughts began. I'm not much of a writer but rather an orator. Each piece of this started as spoken words which I first recorded and then transcribed and refined. In this way, I am able to connect my talents to Torah, as living conversation.

Sefer Devarim, often called Mishneh Torah, the “second telling” of the Torah, has always stood out to me as more than a review. In it, Hashem, through Moshe Rabbeinu, reframes the Torah’s deepest lessons, speaking not to history alone but directly to the Jewish heart.

This project grew out of questions and encouragement, from friends, mentors, and fellow seekers who share a similar hashkafah, yet also wrestle with that focal question: How do I connect with Hashem? Is it about my own journey, or about others? How do I live as a Jew in a complex and changing world?

Throughout this journey, I’ve woven together the teachings of many Rabbanim I’ve learned from, especially my two most direct and influential teachers, Rabbi Yehoshua Gerzi and Rabbi Don Channen, whose wisdom, authenticity, and depth have guided both my connection with Hashem in a practical but heartfelt way.

The goal of Diburim is simple: to help each reader find themselves within the words of Devarim, to make mitzvot personal, to draw Hashem’s presence into daily life, and to turn Torah learning into a living, breathing relationship.

As Sefer Devarim bridges the Torah’s story toward entry into Eretz Yisrael, so too Diburim seeks to bridge reflection and renewal, from self to surrender, from speech to connection and from a me focussed reality to a them focussed reality.

Interestingly, this is my first attempt at such a work and as feedback from my friends and mentors have reflected, even I see the change in myself from parsha to parsha, activity to activity and goal to goal. I hope you all find as much growth in this work and reading it as I have experienced in putting it together.

From Self to Surrender: Walking the Journey of Devarim

Sefer Devarim is more than the closing of the Torah — it is a mirror that reflects who we are and who we are becoming. From Moshe Rabbeinu’s final words to our own preparation for Elul and Tishrei, the sefer guides us from self-awareness to self-transcendence, from ownership to offering, from ego to emunah.

Each parsha in Devarim poses a simple but searching question: Where am I in relation to Hashem’s will? Through Moshe’s review and rebuke, we are reminded that the struggles of the desert — fear, complaint, forgetfulness — still echo within us, yet so too do the faith and gratitude that carried us forward.

As we read Devarim in Elul, the words become tools for cheshbon hanefesh — a spiritual language for return and renewal. The flow of the sefer mirrors the inner journey:

Devarim opens with memory and responsibility.

Va’etchanan calls us to uproot inner idolatry.

Eikev turns our focus to the “small” mitzvot.

Re’eh teaches generosity and awareness.

Shoftim and Ki Tetzei provide Elul’s structure.

Ki Tavo and Nitzavim culminate in gratitude and unity.

From there, we arrive at the Yamim Nora’im and Sukkot — living out what we’ve learned. By Simchat Torah, we’ve not just finished the Torah; we’ve completed a circle of growth.

How to Use This Kuntres

This kuntres is not just a commentary, but a guide for reflection and connection. Each parsha closes with brief questions and practices, simple prompts to translate insight into action. Take them slowly. Let the words meet you where you are. This is the journey from self to surrender.

PART I: THE PARSHIYOT OF SEFER DEVARIM

CHAPTER 1

PARASHAT DEVARIM — Not Just Their Story, Ours Too

This week's parsha, Parshat Devarim, is the opening of the final book of the Torah — Sefer Devarim. It's not just a new parsha; it marks a dramatic shift in tone and perspective.

Here, Moshe Rabbeinu stands at the end of his life. He's not commanding the people with new laws. Instead, he's speaking personally — from the heart. What we hear in these chapters is what many mefarshim describe as Moshe's "ethical will," his final words to a generation poised to enter the land of Israel without him.

Rav Yisroel Gordon zt"l of Los Angeles used to call Sefer Devarim "Moshe Rabbeinu's Last Will and Testament." That's exactly what it is. Moshe knows the end is near. He gathers Bnei Yisrael — like a grandfather calling his family to his bedside — and begins to speak.

But what does he say?

He doesn't tell them, "Everything will be fine." He doesn't sugarcoat history. He starts with tochacha, rebuke. He reminds them of all the ways that the nation failed in the Midbar: the sin of the Meraglim, the complaints, the power struggles, the hesitations, the missed opportunities.

And yet — this new generation was not there. These weren't the ones who cried on the night of Tisha B'Av after the Meraglim. They weren't the ones who asked for meat or rebelled against Moshe. All of that took place decades earlier, mostly within the first two years after leaving Egypt. Those who participated have already died in the desert.

So why is Moshe rebuking this generation? Because this is not just history. This is memory — and in Judaism, memory is not passive. It's a living inheritance.

Like a Grandfather on His Deathbed

Think of a father or grandfather lying on their bed, surrounded by family, about to leave this world. He doesn't just tell his children stories. He shares experiences, values, and warnings. He says, "This is what we went through. This is where we stumbled. Don't make the same mistakes." There's no anger. There's no shame. There's just the deep hope that the next generation will learn from the past.

Moshe is doing the same. He's telling this generation: "You're about to enter the land. You'll face challenges. And I want you to remember — even your parents and grandparents, who saw open miracles, who had Hashem right in front of them — they still fell. Don't be arrogant. Don't be naïve. Learn from them."

Not Shame — Strength

Moshe doesn't tell them this to belittle or berate them. He tells them this to empower them. Yes, even those who had direct access to Hashem — who stood at Har Sinai, who ate the mann, who drank from Miriam's well — even they were human. Even they failed. So don't assume you're above failing. And don't be ashamed of their failures either. Embrace them. Learn from them. Be strengthened by them.

This is the Torah's view of national memory. It isn't edited or whitewashed. We include the hard parts — and we own them.

Viduy: We and Our Fathers

We see this especially in viduy, our confessional prayer. Whether said daily or a few times a year, we include the line: "Aval anachnu v'avoteinu chatanu" (אבל אנחנו ואבותינו חטאנו) — "But we and our fathers have sinned." Why do we confess our ancestors' sins? Because the Torah teaches us that we're not disconnected individuals floating in time. We are part of a chain, bound by memory and mission. The past shapes us — and we carry its lessons forward. It's not about guilt. It's about honesty.

"Ki ein anachnu azei fanim u'kshei oref lomar… Tzaddikim anachnu v'lo chatanu…" (כי אין אנחנו עזי פנים וקשי ערף לומר... צדיקים אנחנו ולא חטאנו) — "We are not brazen-faced or stiff-necked to say: We are righteous and have not sinned…" No — we acknowledge what we've done. And we also acknowledge what those before us did. That's part of what keeps us grounded, humble, and on track.

Preparing for Eretz Yisrael — and for Tisha B'Av

Moshe's message is especially relevant as we approach Tisha B'Av. We know this is a time of mourning — for the Temples, for exile, for tragedies across Jewish history. But it's also a time of truth. We remind ourselves, year after year, not just of what happened — but of why it happened. We review the sins that led to destruction, not to crush ourselves with guilt, but to awaken ourselves to the task ahead.

Eretz Yisrael is not just a gift. It's a responsibility. The Torah calls it "a land that vomits out its inhabitants" if they become corrupt. We have to be worthy of it.

Moshe is telling us: "You are going to inherit the land. Don't inherit it blindly. Inherit it with eyes wide open. Know what happened before — and choose better."

Final Message

As we head into Shabbat Chazon, the Shabbat before Tisha B'Av, we're asked to look deeply at our past and also forward to our future. Yes, there have been failures. But there has also been teshuvah. And hope. And rebuilding. And return.

Moshe Rabbeinu's final message to the people — and to us — is not one of despair. It's a call to responsibility. And a vote of confidence. "You know what happened before. You've seen the consequences. Now take the next step. And do it better."

May this Shabbos be not just a time of mourning, but of vision. A Shabbat of chazon — of clarity. A Shabbat where we carry the past with us not as a burden — but as a compass. And may we merit to rebuild.

Reflection Questions

What patterns from my past keep repeating? What am I being called to learn from them?

Where in my life am I refusing to "own" my family or community's history?

How can I carry the lessons of the past as a compass rather than a burden?

Shabbat Shalom.

CHAPTER 2

PARASHAT VA'ETCHANAN — Climbing Out of the Shadows of Avodah Zarah

Parashat Va'etchanan is packed with foundational themes: Avodah Zarah (idolatry), the repetition of the Aseret HaDibrot (Ten Commandments), and the Shema. While these sections are often viewed in isolation, there's a deep thread connecting them — a spiritual journey upward, guiding us from the lowest human impulses to the highest levels of Divine connection.

Let's begin with Avodah Zarah. Classically, idolatry is understood as the worship of foreign gods. But the Ba'al Shem Tov and other Chassidic masters redefine it as anything we place between ourselves and Hashem. Anger, for example, is described as a form of idolatry — when we lose our temper, we are declaring that our will is supreme, that reality should bend to our desires, not Hashem's. The Gemara (Shabbat 105b) tells us: "Kol ha-ko'es, ke'ilu oved avodah zarah" (כל הכועס כאילו עובד עבודה זרה) — "Anyone who gets angry, it is as if they have worshipped idols."

The Gemara further teaches (Avodah Zarah 12a) that even the appearance of idolatry is prohibited. If someone bends down to remove a thorn in front of an idol, even unintentionally, it's problematic if onlookers could misconstrue the act. Why such strictness? Because Ani Hashem Elokecha — "I am Hashem your God" (Devarim 5:6) — demands that we live with constant awareness of Hashem's presence. The path to true emunah requires radical honesty and vigilance over even the subtlest disconnects.

There is another layer to why this matters so urgently: we are not private souls wandering alone — we are a holy people with a holy job. The Torah calls Klal Yisrael a "mamlechet kohanim v'goy kadosh" (ממלכת כהנים וגוי קדוש) (Exodus 19:6) and the prophets envision us as an "or lagoyim" (אור לגויים) — a light unto the nations (Isaiah 42:6).

That mission means our inner life carries public weight: our anger, jealousy, and petty idolatries not only harm our character but dim the witness we are meant to bring into the world. The commandments, the Shema, and the whole moral architecture of the Torah are training us to be visibly different — not in order to withdraw, but in order to model a way of life that points others toward Hashem. In short: holiness is both personal purification and public service; failing in one weakens the other.

Let's now return to the Aseret HaDibrot, the Ten Commandments. They open with the highest statement of truth — Hashem as our Redeemer from Mitzrayim — but they conclude on what seems like a much more "human" level: Lo Tachmod — Do not covet.

At first glance, jealousy seems far less severe than idolatry or murder. But perhaps that's exactly the point. Coveting arises from a distorted vision — a life lived through the eyes of "what I lack" rather than "what Hashem has given me." It's a fundamentally self-centered worldview, one that can spiral into resentment, dishonesty, and yes, even idolatry.

As Rashi explains on Bamidbar (Numbers) 15:39: "העין רואה והלב חומד" — "The eye sees and the heart desires." The Torah warns us that spiritual downfall often begins not with the outward act, but with what we allow into our gaze: vision shapes desire, and desire, unchecked, too often shapes action.

Yet the ladder of the Aseret HaDibrot offers a way up. After jealousy, the previous commandment is Lo Tirtzach — Do not murder. As jarring as it sounds, this is already a step above jealousy. Why? Because it's no longer just inner emotion — it's action, however misguided. From there, the commandments move upward through theft, false witness, and ultimately to Kibbud Av Va'eim, the honoring of parents — the first (as we work backwards) "positive" commandment that builds trust in societal and spiritual structure.

Above this is Shabbat, the sanctification of time and the affirmation that Hashem is the Creator. And from there, we reach the peak: "Anochi Hashem Elokecha" — total recognition of Divine unity and providence.

But Va'etchanan doesn't stop there. It immediately continues into the Shema, perhaps the Torah's clearest declaration of Divine oneness:

"Shema Yisrael, Hashem Elokeinu, Hashem Echad." (שמע ישראל ה' אלהינו ה' אחד)

The Gemara in Berachot (13b) teaches that when we say "Echad," we should expand the word. Many commentators explain this to mean to reflect on Hashem's unity in all realms — heaven, earth, all directions.

The third letter is Daled, numerical value "four," which denotes the four directions of the horizontal plane: north, south, east, west. Chet, numerical value "eight," signifies the seven heavens and the earth, the vertical plane, including all spiritual dimensions. Aleph, which has the numerical value "one," refers to G‑d Himself. Everything we experience, every challenge or joy, is part of that.

The Shema invites us to take everything we've learned — from the dangers of idolatry, to the self-discipline of the Ten Commandments — and internalize it until it becomes our essence. Not just obedience, but devotion. Not just avoiding sin, but becoming a vessel for Hashem's presence in the world.

The Avot — Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov — are described as the Merkavah, the chariot of the Divine. They lived in such harmony with Hashem's will that they became vehicles of it. That level is daunting. But the Torah believes we can climb there — step by step, dibrah by dibrah, kri'ah by kri'ah.

And so we ask ourselves this week:

Am I still at the level of desire and jealousy? Am I struggling with emotional reactions like anger or resentment? Am I moving into action — building positive habits, sanctifying my time, honoring my parents, recognizing Hashem's gifts?

Because only by climbing these steps can we arrive at the true Ani Hashem Elokecha, and from there, to the clarity and peace of Shema Yisrael.

Reflection Questions

Am I still at the level of desire and jealousy, or am I moving toward recognizing Hashem's gifts?

What "small" idolatries do I place between myself and Hashem? (Anger, resentment, control?)

When I say the Shema, do I truly reflect on Hashem's unity in all directions of my life?

CHAPTER 3

PARASHAT EIKEV — Don't Step on the Small Things

This week's parasha, Eikev, is filled with amazing little messages — and if you'll excuse the pun, they shouldn't be "stepped on." The very word eikev means "heel." Rashi (Devarim 7:12, s.v. vehaya eikev tishme'un) tells us that this hints to mitzvot that people tend to tread upon with their heels — mitzvot that are easy to forget, that we step over without even thinking, the things that seem so small or insignificant that they barely register in our minds.

But why are these "heel mitzvot" so important? If we think back to last week's parasha, Va'etchanan, we read the Shema — the moment where we declare that my will is nothing compared to Hashem's will, and my goal is to be mevatel (nullify) my own ratzon to His ratzon. If I'm truly in that mindset, then who am I to decide which mitzvah matters to Hashem and which one doesn't? The truth is, Hashem has already told us what matters. He gave us the Torah, the Shulchan Aruch, the Mishnah Berurah, and the wisdom of our sages to guide us. These mitzvot — even the ones that seem small — are part of His plan for us. If they're in the Torah, they matter.

Bringing the small into awareness

The real question is: if these mitzvot are so easy to forget, how do we bring them back into our conscious awareness? The Baal Shem Tov teaches that hashgacha pratit — Individual Divine Providence — is revealed in our lives to the degree that we are aware of the small details of our actions. When a Jew trains himself to notice and sanctify even the smallest moments, he opens himself to seeing Hashem's hand everywhere.

I once learned this teaching through an example connected to the mikveh. When preparing to immerse, a chossid asked his Rebbi, what kavanot should I have when going to the mikve. The Rebbe responded based on this teaching to start being aware even before you get near the water. As you take off your shoes, think: "I am taking off my shoes in preparation for the mikveh." When you remove your socks, think: "I am removing my socks in preparation for going into the mikve." Step by step, be aware everything you are doing and that what you are doing is part of a holy act. Why? Because as Hashem said to Moshe Rabbeinu to relay to the Jewish People, "You shall be holy, for I, your G-d, am holy." (קדשים תהיו כי קדוש אני ה' אלהיכם) (Vayikra 19:2). When we learn to pay attention to these small acts, not just the "big" mitzvot but the little ones, we bring them to the forefront of our minds. They stop being background noise and start being acts of connection to Hashem.

Even the way you tie your shoes

Halachah itself reflects this mindset. The Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 2:4) teaches that there is an order for putting on shoes: right shoe first, then left, but tie the left first (Shabbos 61a), as a reminder of the way we bind tefillin on our left arm. Think about that: something as mundane as putting on your shoes can remind you of the covenant between you and Hashem. This is a perfect example of a "heel mitzvah", a small, almost hidden moment that can elevate your day. When I live with that awareness, the little things start to matter more and more. And when they matter to me, Hashem says: "If My small things matter to you, then you matter to Me."

The reward — and the warning

The Torah promises: "And it will be, because you will listen to these ordinances and keep them… Hashem your God will keep for you the covenant and the kindness… and He will love you and bless you and multiply you" (והיה עקב תשמעון... ושמר ה' אלהיך לך את הברית ואת החסד... ואהבך וברכך והרבך) (Devarim 7:12–13).

But Moshe also warns: "Lest you eat and be satisfied… and your heart will grow haughty, and you will forget Hashem your God" (פן תאכל ושבעת... ורם לבבך ושכחת את ה' אלהיך) (Devarim 8:12–14). The sefarim (and can be seen plainly in life) explain that when material blessings increase, there is a spiritual danger, we become distracted, and the small mitzvot are often the first to slip away. When that happens, Hashem may take away the blessing, not necessarily as a punishment, but as a loving reminder to reset, to bring us back to humility and awareness.

From the heel to the head — together

Later in the parasha we read Vehaya Im Shamoa (והיה אם שמע), the second paragraph of the Shema (Devarim 11:13–21). Many of the phrases echo the first paragraph, but there's a key difference: the first paragraph speaks in the singular (bechol levavcha - בכל לבבך), focusing on the individual's relationship with Hashem. The second paragraph speaks in the plural (bechol levavchem - בכל לבבכם), addressing the nation as a whole.

Rashi comments that bechol levavchem now implies the unity of everyone's hearts where previously it was on the individual. When we learn to value the small mitzvot, we also learn to value the "small" people, those who might be the "heels" of the nation, as us all having unified "hearts". The head and the heel are both essential to the body. The leaders and the simplest Jews are equally precious to Hashem. When we come together with our hearts, souls, and might united, then the blessings of Hashem can be complete.

So the message is simple, but it changes everything: Don't step on the little things. Whether it's a "small" mitzvah, a "small" person, or a "small" detail of life, Hashem treasures it all. If it matters to Him, it should matter to us. And when we live that way, we become the people He wants us to be — from the head to the heel.

Reflection Questions

Which "heel mitzvot" have I been stepping over? What small observances have I forgotten?

How can I bring more awareness to mundane moments today?

Who are the "small people" in my life that I've been overlooking or undervaluing?

Shabbat Shalom.

CHAPTER 4

PARASHAT RE'EH — Bracha, Avodah Zarah, and Tzedakah as One Path

Parshat Re'eh is packed with running themes that flow side by side. We begin with a dramatic and almost theatrical moment: the division of the tribes. Six tribes are stationed on Har Gerizim, six tribes on Har Eval, and the Levi'im together with the Kohanim stand in the valley between them. From that central place, they proclaim blessings to one side and curses to the other (Devarim 27:11–13). It's an image that sets the tone — the people literally positioned between bracha and klala.

But then the parsha moves quickly into other themes: strong warnings not to imitate the nations of the land, not to fall into the trap of avodah zarah, not to scar ourselves, not to distort Hashem's service. And finally, woven throughout, there is the recurring theme of giving: tzedakah, ma'aser, and supporting those in need.

At first glance, these might seem like three different topics: bracha and klala, avoiding avodah zarah, and giving tzedakah. But if we look closely, the Torah is interweaving them together into one continuous lesson for us.

Bracha and Klala – Two Perspectives on the Same Reality

The seforim on this concept make a powerful point: there isn't really such a thing as a klala in the absolute sense. There is revealed bracha — blessing that we can see and feel right away — and there is bracha that is not yet revealed, which appears to us as curse. In other words, what seems like klala is ultimately Hashem's way of redirecting us, warning us, correcting us.

A few weeks ago, we mentioned the idea that a klala can be understood as a kind of fatherly warning. If you see your child walking toward danger, you raise your voice, you stop them, you may even take something away from them. In that moment, the child may experience it as harshness, as restriction, but later they understand it was an act of love. So too, Hashem gives us brachot that are open and sweet, and He also gives us reminders — which might look like klalot — that exist to keep us on the straight path.

So even at the beginning of the parsha, when half of the nation is facing Har Gerizim and half facing Har Eval, it's not that half the people are "bad" and half are "good." Rather, Hashem is laying before us the reality of life: we always stand between revealed blessing and hidden blessing.

The question is how we will see it, how we will interpret it, and whether we will allow those reminders to guide us.

Avodah Zarah – The Illusion of "Mine"

This perspective prepares us for the next great theme of the parsha: the command to avoid avodah zarah. Over and over, the Torah insists: "Do not be like the nations, do not serve their gods, do not follow their ways." Why? Because to be a Jew, first and foremost, means to know that Hashem is everything. Ein od milvado (אין עוד מלבדו). There is nothing else besides Him (Devarim 4:35).

When we forget this — when we believe our power, our success, our wealth is our own — then we start slipping into idolatry. The Gemara in Sanhedrin (64a) tells us that when Hashem removed the desire for avodah zarah, that destructive drive was replaced with a powerful desire for money.

In other words, the way people once related to idols — as ultimate sources of security, meaning, or identity — is now the way many people relate to wealth.

So when the Torah warns us against avodah zarah, it is not only talking about bowing down to statues. It is also warning us against bowing down to ourselves, to our own egos, to the illusion that "my strength and the might of my hand made me this wealth" (Devarim 8:17). That too is a form of idolatry.

Tzedakah and Ma'aser – Returning to Hashem What Is Already His

This brings us straight into the mitzvot of tzedakah and ma'aser. The Torah commands us to support the poor, the orphan, the widow, and the Levite who has no portion in the land. And Chazal elevate tzedakah to one of the greatest mitzvot, teaching that:

"Tzedakah and acts of kindness are the equivalent of all the mitzvot of the Torah" – Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 1:1

"Greater is tzedakah than all the sacrifices" – Talmud, Sukkah 49b

"If only the people who lived in the generation of the Flood and the people of Sodom had given tzedakah, they would not have perished" – Midrash Zutta, Song of Songs 1

"Great is tzedakah, for since the day that the world was created until this day the world stands upon tzedakah" – Midrash Tanna d'Vei Eliyahu Zutta 1

"Tzedakah saves from death" – Mishlei 10:2

Why does tzedakah have such power? Because giving corrects the illusion of idolatry. Giving breaks the ego that says, "It's mine."

Pirkei Avot (3:7) says: "Give Him from His own, for you and what is yours are His." (תן לו משלו שאתה ושלך שלו) When I give, I am not losing something that was mine. I am returning to Hashem what was already His in the first place.

The Torah itself emphasizes this: "It is Hashem Who gives you the strength to make wealth" (והוא הנתן לך כח לעשות חיל) (Devarim 8:18). My talents, my opportunities, my ability to work, the rain that makes crops grow, the economy that enables me to profit — all of it is a gift. Hashem says: I give you 100%, and I ask you to hold onto 90%. The other 10% — give it forward, to My people, to those I love, to those who cannot provide for themselves.

In this way, ma'aser and tzedakah are like modern korbanot. In the Beit HaMikdash, the fat and blood of the korban symbolized our own life-force, offered back to Hashem. Today, our money represents our "blood, sweat, and tears" — the work of our hands, our energy, our time. When we give it away, we are symbolically offering ourselves.

And unlike the nations who scar themselves or cut themselves as part of their rituals (Devarim 14:1), we serve Hashem in a healthy way: by giving, by supporting, by elevating. We don't harm ourselves; we lift others up.

Bracha or Klala – It's How We See

When I remember that money is a gift from Hashem, then my wealth becomes a bracha. When I forget, and I clutch it tightly, declaring "It's mine," then it turns into a klala. Not because Hashem wants to punish me, but because I have blinded myself to the Source, and I need to be reminded.

Like a parent who withholds something from a child not to hurt them but to protect them, Hashem sometimes sends us difficulties to bring us back. The Ramban explains that even what we perceive as curses are truly forms of divine love, designed to refine us and guide us.

And that circles back to the opening word of the parsha: Re'eh (ראה) — See. Hashem says: "See, I place before you today blessing and curse" (ראה אנכי נתן לפניכם היום ברכה וקללה) (Devarim 11:26). See — with your own eyes — that everything comes from Me. See that the choice is not about whether you will encounter blessing or curse, but about how you will understand and live with them.

Conclusion

So the parsha weaves together three themes into one message:

Bracha and klala — life contains both, but both come from Hashem.

Avodah zarah — idolatry is the illusion that something else is in control, especially money.

Tzedakah and ma'aser — the antidote to idolatry, the act of returning to Hashem what is already His.

When we live this way, when we give generously, when we remember Ein Od Milvado, when we see challenges as hidden blessings — then we are truly standing on the mountain, in the place of bracha.

May we merit to always see Hashem's hand in everything, to give with joy, and to transform all that we have into revealed blessing.

Reflection Questions

When I look at challenges in my life, can I reframe them as hidden blessings?

Do I treat my resources as "mine" or as gifts from Hashem to steward?

What would it look like to give tzedakah not out of obligation, but out of joy and gratitude?

Shabbat Shalom.

PARASHAT SHOFTIM — Law, Order, and Holiness in the Everyday

Elul Connection – Ani L'dodi

We've just entered the month of Elul, a month known for preparation before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The Sages teach that the very name Elul is hinted in the verse "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li" (אני לדודי ודודי לי) — I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (Shir HaShirim 6:3).

This reminds us that our Avodat Hashem is not only about rules or fear of judgment, but about a relationship of love. Just as in a marriage, there are times when we do something not because it makes sense to us, but because our spouse desires it — so too with Hashem. There are mitzvot we cannot fully explain (chukim), yet we fulfill them as an act of devotion and love.

But Elul also reminds us that love is not enough on its own. A marriage also needs structure and order. There are times when we want things to make sense, or at least to see how they may shape life meaningfully. This is exactly where Parshat Shoftim comes in — providing the framework for a holy society.

Shoftim – Human Justice and Structure

This week, however, Parshat Shoftim opens from a different perspective. The very name — Shoftim, Judges — already brings us into the practical, human reality of how to structure society. It's not only about avoiding idolatry or foreign practices; it's about building a just and holy community.

"Shoftim v'shotrim titen lecha" (שפטים ושטרים תתן לך) — "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your gates" (Devarim 16:18). It is a mitzvah to establish courts and law enforcement in Eretz Yisrael, so that society does not descend into chaos (Sanhedrin 16b, Rambam Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:1).

As someone who grew up in America, I sometimes think of the "Wild West," where justice was inconsistent, duels took place in the street, and sheriffs often looked the other way. The Torah tells us: don't let that happen. Even something as "basic" as setting up judges and officers is in fact a godly act.

Impartial Justice – The Judge's Responsibility

The Torah emphasizes again and again the importance of impartial justice: "You shall not favor the poor, nor honor the great; with righteousness shall you judge your fellow" (לא תשא פני דל ולא תהדר פני גדול בצדק תשפט עמיתך) (Vayikra 19:15, cf. Devarim 1:17).

Pirkei Avot expands on this: a judge must not tilt judgment either way — not favoring the poor out of pity, and not honoring the wealthy out of respect. Justice must be blind.

The Torah goes further: "You shall not take a bribe" (לא תקח שחד) (Devarim 16:19). Rashi notes that even if the bribe would not change the outcome — even if the judge was going to rule the same way — he must remove himself from the case. Why? Because a bribe clouds perception. A judge who accepts influence, no matter how small, is no longer fit to rule. This is how Am Yisrael remains holy: not just in ritual, but in ensuring that our daily lives, our courts, and our leaders are untouched by corruption.

The King and His Torah

The next step of the things in the world which are normal, but which we need to keep in mind to do in a holy way in the parsha is the question of monarchy: "When you come to the land the Lord, your God, is giving you, and you possess it and live therein, and you say, 'I will set a king over myself, like all the nations around me,'" (כי תבא אל הארץ... ואמרת אשימה עלי מלך ככל הגוים) (Devarim 17:14). This request is not Hashem's ideal — after all, He Himself is our true King — but He permits it, with strict limits.

The king may not accumulate excessive horses, wealth, or wives (Devarim 17:16–17). Unlike the kings of the nations, who seek glory and indulgence, the Jewish king's task is service and humility. To safeguard this, the Torah commands that the king write for himself a personal Sefer Torah and read from it constantly: "So that his heart not be lifted above his brethren" (לבלתי רום לבבו מאחיו) (17:19–20).

The Rambam (Hilchot Melachim 3:1) writes that the king carries this Torah wherever he goes. His authority is never for personal power but only to guide Am Yisrael under the authority of Torah.

These are all to remind us that even a King is still supposed to be subservient to Hashem. Unlike the kings of the nations, who pursue power, honor, and desire, the Jewish king's role is to serve Hashem and guide the people.

Prophets – True and False

Earlier in the Torah, the concern was primarily with Jews falsely claiming to speak in Hashem's name. Here the scope widens: we are warned even against prophets from among the nations, or those who use sorcery and witchcraft to predict the future.

Bilam is the classic example. He truly did hear Hashem's word, but he used it for selfish and corrupt purposes (Bamidbar 22–24). For the reasons of his motive was he brought down and punished, but he never prophesied for the Jews, only for the nations.

The bigger danger we are being warned of here is that prophecy outside of Torah is possible. In this parsha, the Torah contrasts false prophecy and kishuf with the true guidance of nevua and ruach hakodesh given to the Nevi'im of Am Yisrael. We see that while Hashem may choose to speak with some unique people of the nations of the world, even that can be confused with actions of Tumah.

The message is clear: don't be impressed by what looks powerful, mystical, or accurate. Truthfully, we don't even need to entertain those ways because there is always a kosher way, the Torah's way. Not because the other path lacks power, but because it lacks holiness. Just as the Jews had Moshe, Yehoshua and others to lead them then in the way of Torah, we have our guides and leaders now and here as well but just need to learn how to find them.

Witnesses and Testimony

Another foundation of justice in Shoftim is testimony: "By the testimony of two or three witnesses shall a matter be established" (על פי שנים עדים או שלשה עדים יקום דבר) (Devarim 19:15).

This principle ensures that justice is rooted in truth. False witnesses (eidim zomemim) are punished with the very sentence they hoped to impose on another (19:16–19). This safeguard keeps society from crumbling under lies and manipulation. Again, this is something other nations also recognize, but for us, it is not merely civic law — it is kedushah.

War and Bal Tashchit

Shoftim also addresses the laws of warfare. Even in battle, boundaries remain: we may not destroy fruit-bearing trees when laying siege: "For man is like the tree of the field" (כי האדם עץ השדה) (20:19). From here we learn the mitzvah of bal tashchit (בל תשחית) — the prohibition against needless destruction.

Sadly, in recent times we saw the opposite in Gush Katif, when flourishing orchards and greenhouses were destroyed rather than cherished. The Torah tells us: value Hashem's gifts. Even in the chaos of war, we are commanded to build, not destroy.

Further than this, we see another warning in action as well: if we act like those around us, the ones who should not be emulated, we may come to emulate the actions they do, even if they do not make sense in a bad way. We may act out of spite or anger and destroy without purpose, the ultimate descent to animalistic behaviors.

Stepping Out of the Midbar

All of these laws remind us of the transition taking place. Am Yisrael is leaving the midbar, where life was constant miracles — the manna, the clouds of glory, the Mishkan — and entering the land, where they will farm, fight wars, build courts, and appoint leaders.

And the Torah's message is this: holiness is not only in the Beit Midrash or the Mishkan. It must extend to the courtroom, the battlefield, the palace, and the orchard.

Conclusion – Finding Kedushah in the Mundane

This is the thread uniting both Elul and Shoftim. In Elul, we prepare ourselves to renew a relationship of love with Hashem: Ani l'dodi v'dodi li. Sometimes that love moves us to act beyond reason, and sometimes we see the sense and wisdom of Hashem's mitzvot. In Shoftim, we are reminded that even the rational, civic institutions of society — justice, kingship, courts, testimony, and even military conduct — are not just "practical." They are infused with kedushah when done in service of Hashem.

The nations of the world may also have courts, prophets, kings, and armies. But for us, every one of these is elevated — structured not by human whim, but by the Torah.

May we take this into Elul: to find kedushah in the ordinary, to align both our acts of love and our acts of order with the ratzon Hashem, and to enter the Yamim Nora'im ready to live as a truly holy people.

Where in my life do I need to create better boundaries (ma'akeh) to protect holiness?

Am I living with integrity both in public and in private?

How can I bring kedushah into the "ordinary" structures of my day?
