PARASHAT KI TETZEI — A Checklist for Elul

This week's parsha, Ki Tetzei, is truly an amazing parsha. On a personal note, it was my Bar Mitzvah parsha, which already makes it meaningful to me. But beyond that, Ki Tetzei is remarkable because it falls at a very opportune time: we are in Elul, the month of cheshbon ha-nefesh, of taking stock of who I am, where I stand, where my growth has taken me, and where my alignment with Hashem's will should be going forward.

Ki Tetzei is also unique in another way: it is the sixth parsha in Sefer Devarim, which has eleven parshiyot total. That means it stands at the center point of the book. This is a perfect moment to pause, reflect on what has come before, and realign ourselves before moving forward.

A Quick Recap of the Journey in Devarim

In Devarim, Moshe began by reviewing the mistakes of the past and warning us not to repeat them. In Va'etchanan, we were called to align ourselves with Hashem's ratzon, highlighted through the Ten Commandments, from the lowest level of resisting jealousy all the way up to "Anochi Hashem Elokecha." In Eikev, we were reminded not to step on the "small mitzvot" (mitzvot kalot), since we don't know which mitzvot are greater in Hashem's eyes (Rashi to Devarim 7:12). In Re'eh, we were shown how to move beyond selfishness, avoid idolatry, and embrace tzedakah and generosity. In Shoftim, we came down to the practical: establishing justice, structure, and boundaries in society. Now comes Ki Tetzei, the midpoint. With its 74 mitzvot — more than any other parsha — it provides a practical checklist for daily living.

Derech Eretz as the Foundation

Pirkei Avot 3:17 teaches: "Rabbi Eliezer the son of Azariah said: If there is no Torah, there is no derech eretz; if there is no derech eretz, there is no Torah." (אם אין תורה אין דרך ארץ אם אין דרך ארץ אין תורה) Pirkei Avot (3:10) also teaches: "One who is pleasing to his fellow men, is pleasing to G‑d. But one who is not pleasing to his fellow men, is not pleasing to G‑d." Our parsha is filled with mitzvot that emphasize how we live with one another, not just our private service of Hashem.

The parsha opens with the laws of the captive woman (eshet yefat to'ar). The Torah recognizes that in the heat of war, human passions are inflamed. Instead of pretending this doesn't exist, the Torah regulates it. The requirement to bring her home, remove the external beauty, and wait a full month (Devarim 21:12–13, Rashi ad loc.) is not a punishment to her — it is a reset for him. It forces the soldier to step back from adrenaline and passion into calm reflection: "Am I truly choosing this relationship in reality, or was it only in the heat of the moment?" This law speaks not only to desire but to responsibility: Am I building my home on a foundation of holiness or selfishness?

Immediately afterward comes the law of the hated wife and then the rebellious son (ben sorer u'moreh). Chazal (Sanhedrin 71a) point out the progression: if one's household is built without proper love and alignment, it spirals into hatred and eventually destructive children. The Torah is not just giving laws; it is teaching us to pause and ask: What kind of home am I building?

From the Home to Society

The second aliyah emphasizes dignity even in judgment: even one executed by the court must be buried respectfully (Devarim 21:23). Then come hashavat aveidah (returning lost property) and prikah u'te'ina (helping lift a fallen animal) — mitzvot that force us to look outward and help others, even those we may not like (Rambam, Hilchot Gezeilah Va'Aveidah 11:3). We are even commanded to show compassion to animals with shiluach haken — sending away the mother bird before taking her chicks (Devarim 22:6–7). The Ramban explains this is not about the bird's feelings, but about cultivating compassion within us, training us to act with mercy in every area of life.

Then comes the mitzvah to build a ma'akeh (fence) around a roof (Devarim 22:8). Chazal see this as more than architecture: it's about creating healthy boundaries in life. It's not a wall to keep people out; it's a guardrail to protect those already inside our homes. The Gemara (Bava Kama 15b) expands this principle to every dangerous situation: we must take responsibility to remove hazards and protect others.

The Broader Checklist

As the parsha continues, we encounter mitzvot that cover almost every aspect of human life:

Kilayim and sha'atnez — avoiding improper mixtures (Devarim 22:9–11)

Tzitzit — constant reminders of Hashem's mitzvot (22:12, Menachot 43b)

Giluy arayot — prohibited relationships, setting boundaries in holiness

Moving boundary markers — respecting property and not imposing on others (Devarim 19:14, reaffirmed here)

Justice in business — honest weights and measures (25:13–16, Rambam Hilchot Geneivah 7:1)

Kindness to workers, converts, orphans, and widows (24:14–22)

Altogether, Ki Tetzei is like a spiritual mirror: Am I treating others with dignity? Am I acting responsibly at home and in business? Am I setting boundaries that protect life and holiness? Am I remembering the vulnerable, those who are easily forgotten, and lifting them up or am I finding the shortcuts in life to capture small pennies from others?

Preparing for Rosh Hashanah

All of this is given now, in Elul. Just as Ani L'dodi V'dodi Li (Shir HaShirim 6:3) reminds us that Hashem is close and I should be putting the wants and will of my beloved before me and my beloved will also keep my wants and will in front of her, Ki Tetzei provides the practical checklist for the cheshbon hanefesh of this month and helps me prepare for a sweeter coming year.

We are only a few weeks away from Rosh Hashanah, the day when we proclaim: "Hayom harat olam, hayom ya'amid bamishpat kol yetzurei olam" — today is the birthday of the world, today all creatures stand in judgment.

So the question Ki Tetzei pushes us to ask is: Am I living with derech eretz? Am I honoring my family, helping my fellow, caring for the vulnerable, and creating healthy boundaries in my life? Because when we do, we are not just preparing for Rosh Hashanah — we are preparing to stand before Hashem with lives that reflect His image.

Reflection Questions

Am I treating others—family, neighbors, strangers—with the dignity they deserve?

Where am I taking shortcuts or "capturing small pennies" at the expense of ethics?

What healthy boundaries do I need to establish in my relationships and home?

Shabbat Shalom.

PARASHAT KI TAVO — Coming In with Gratitude

This week's parashah opens with "Ki tavo el ha'aretz" — when one comes into the land. Last week, in Ki Teitzei, we read "Ki teitzei" — when one goes out. The difference is meaningful. Going out is about facing the world, meeting its challenges and tests. Coming in is about arrival, reflection, and gratitude.

Going out focuses on action: how one behaves, treats others, and upholds Torah values under pressure. Coming in is about pausing, reflecting, and taking stock of how one has acted. It's a moment to recognize what has been achieved and to feel gratitude for the gifts and guidance that made it possible.

Bikurim — Personal Gratitude

The parashah begins with the mitzvah of Bikurim, bringing the first fruits to the Beit HaMikdash (Devarim 26:1–11). These fruits are the seven species special to Eretz Yisrael: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates (Devarim 8:7–10; Sifrei Devarim 259). The mitzvah isn't just about giving thanks in general — it's personal.

Imagine a child saying, "Thank you, Dad, for this chocolate." If the chocolate was random or purchased without thought, the thanks is polite but distant. But if the child thanks the parent for something made or carefully chosen — a meal, a snack, or a fun day planned just for them — the gratitude is personal, heartfelt, and meaningful. Bikurim works the same way: it transforms thanks into a recognition of Hashem's care and the specialness of the gifts received.

Joy is also connected to clarity. The Gemara teaches that happiness grows when doubt is removed (Berachot 31a). Midrashically, the letters of safek (ס־פ־ק) add up to the same value as Amalek (ע־מ־ל־ק): both equal 240. Doubt (safek) creates a space for Amalek to enter; removing doubt allows true joy to flourish. When there is no safek, there is joy.

Victory That Matters

The parashah reminds us that true victory isn't just about overcoming the outside world. Real success is measured by how one behaves along the way — with integrity, compassion, and restraint. Coming home after challenges isn't about survival or results alone; it's about reflecting on conduct and ethical growth.

Har Gerizim and Har Eval — Choosing Blessing

Later, the Torah describes standing on Har Gerizim and Har Eval for blessings and curses (Devarim 27). One mountain is fertile and green, the other more barren. The division teaches that blessings and warnings are real, and perspective matters.

As we explored in Parshat Re'eh, the choice between blessing and curse isn't always what it appears. Here in Ki Tavo, the lesson deepens: the experience of rebuke and reflection is deeply relational.

The Mitteler Rebbe's experience during the reading of the Tochachah illustrates this profoundly. According to Chassidic accounts, he fainted when the rebuke was read — not because the content was new, but because his father, the Alter Rebbe, was absent. Normally, the Alter Rebbe's presence provided guidance and context, allowing the teachings to be received with clarity and calm. Without that stabilizing influence, the intensity of the words was overwhelming.

This story teaches that the experience of rebuke and reflection is deeply relational. When self-examination has already been undertaken, even harsh words become constructive. Rebuke is transformed from fear into guidance, offering a path toward ethical refinement. It also reminds us that presence — guidance, mentorship, and proper context — is crucial in spiritual growth.

Gratitude for Life in Eretz Yisrael

Toward the end of the parashah, the focus turns to deep, personal gratitude — hakarat hatov — for the gift of living in Israel. There is clarity about friends and foes, and a sense of safety in knowing who one can trust. This allows for reflection and thanksgiving, especially in contrast to situations elsewhere.

Part of the blessing of Eretz Yisrael is living under a system where Torah values shape justice. The Torah recognizes that disagreements exist and that good and bad are not always clear-cut. But it strictly prohibits taking the law into one's own hands. Individuals are never judge, jury, and executioner. The Torah, especially in Parshat Shoftim (Devarim 16–17), lays out proper process, witnesses, and courts.

When we see examples — whether in our own time or throughout history — of societies where justice breaks down, where people act as their own judges, where violence replaces due process, it deepens our gratitude for a land and legal system rooted in Torah principles. For example, recently in the United States, someone was murdered simply for speaking their mind — for encouraging others to think and engage in discussion. Such tragedies remind us that the breakdown of proper justice endangers everyone.

This contrast highlights the blessing of living in a land and society where personal safety and ethical structure are supported by Torah law. It deepens gratitude for the gift of Eretz Yisrael and reinforces the lesson of Bikurim: acknowledging and celebrating the gifts that Hashem provides. The ability to live safely, reflect, and act with integrity becomes a core part of personal thanks in Ki Tavo.

Offering Personal "First Fruits"

As Elul continues and Selichot approach, the parashah encourages bringing personal "first fruits" — the best of oneself — to Hashem:

Reflect on the past year. What went well? Where is there room to grow?

Remove doubt (safek) by resolving unresolved conflicts or uncertainties.

Offer personal gratitude for specific blessings: guidance, achievements, relationships, protection.

Share gratitude with family, community, or congregation. Recognizing these gifts strengthens the connection to Hashem and makes joy tangible.

Conclusion

Ki Tavo invites reflection and gratitude. After the challenges of "going out," it is time to "come in" and take stock. Joy comes when doubt is removed, clarity prevails, and one recognizes the gifts of life. Gratitude is personal, relational, and deeply connected to everyday life. This parashah reminds that the best way to celebrate life's blessings is through awareness, integrity, and heartfelt thanks — truly bringing the "first fruits" of one's actions, reflections, and experiences back to Hashem.

Reflection Questions

What are my personal "first fruits"—the best of what I can offer to Hashem right now?

What doubt (safek) needs to be removed from my life to allow joy to flourish?

Can I name three specific, personal blessings I've received this year?

PARASHAT NITZAVIM — Standing Together: Hidden Things, Revealed Responsibility

This week's parashah opens with a vivid scene: "You are all standing today before Hashem your God—your heads, your tribes, your elders, your officers, every man of Israel, your little ones, your wives, and the stranger in your camp—from the wood-chopper to the water-drawer—to enter into the covenant of Hashem your God." (אתם נצבים היום כלכם לפני ה' אלהיכם ראשיכם שבטיכם זקניכם ושטריכם כל איש ישראל טפכם נשיכם וגרך אשר בקרב מחניך מחטב עציך עד שאב מימיך) (Deut. 29:9–11)

From the highest leader to the person drawing water, every soul is present. No one is too lofty to be included, and no one is too small to matter. Hashem renews the covenant as we prepare to enter the Land, reminding us that this relationship is not only national but deeply personal.

"Why Am I Responsible?"

Many of us quietly ask this question. I'm one person. Why must my choices, my actions, carry weight for the whole? Rabbi Gerzi teaches that Jews are doers, diggers of wells. We are not meant to let the world simply happen to us; we are called to happen to the world, to carve out spaces of holiness and life-giving water wherever we stand. The covenant demands that each of us become an active participant. From this parsha and from our Rebbeim, we learn: I am responsible. I am a doer, not just a passive observer.

Who Are We Responsible For — and the Silent Tochacha

Chazal teach, "Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh" (כל ישראל ערבים זה בזה) — all of Israel are guarantors for one another (Shevuot 39a). Responsibility isn't abstract. The Torah continues, "The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things are for us and our children forever, to do all the words of this Torah" (הנסתרת לה' אלהינו והנגלת לנו ולבנינו עד עולם) (Devarim 29:28). We are not judged for what is truly hidden, but once wrongdoing becomes public—or once we have the ability to guide someone—we share in the duty to act.

The mitzvah of tochachah (rebuke) gives this responsibility a practical framework: "You shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him" (הוכח תוכיח את עמיתך ולא תשא עליו חטא) (Vayikra 19:17). Chazal (Arakhin 16b) teach that true rebuke must be gentle and constructive, aimed at helping, not humiliating. If I know how to speak in a way that might reach someone, I am obligated to try.

But tochachah is more than words. The Rambam notes that living with integrity—showing kindness, honesty, and faithfulness—is itself a silent rebuke and a model for others. How I carry myself "in the street" is often the strongest tochachah of all. Simply by acting with dignity, responsibility, and even safety (like wearing a bicycle helmet to model caution), I help lift the people around me.

Hidden and Revealed

Nitzavim acknowledges the limits of our reach: "The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things are for us and our children forever, to fulfill all the words of this Torah." (Deut. 29:28) If someone secretly hides an idol under the bed, that is for God alone to judge. But when wrongdoing becomes public—when it shapes the moral texture of the community—the responsibility becomes ours. The Talmud teaches, Kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh — all Israel are guarantors for one another (Shavuot 39a). Blessings and curses are addressed to the entire nation because covenantal life is shared life. We see this principle in the story of Rachel hiding her father Lavan's teraphim (Gen. 31). Jacob cannot be punished for what he does not know. Only the one who acts in secret faces that private judgment. But once sin is visible, silence is complicity.

Integrity of the Heart

The Torah calls us to a wholeness that spans private and public. Shiviti Hashem lenegdi tamid (שויתי ה' לנגדי תמיד) — "I place Hashem before me always" (Ps. 16:8). Whether people are watching or not, our lives must reflect God's presence. Our private selves must match the image we project in the synagogue, the workplace, or the street. Rambam (Hilchot De'ot 6:7) frames this as a mitzvah of tochachah — offering gentle, constructive guidance — because only a community of integrity can sustain the covenant.

Growth That Flows Outward

Personal growth in Torah is never only for self-perfection — it's about us growing to help others and growing with others as well. We refine ourselves so that we can lift others. Study turns into prayer; prayer flows into acts of tzedakah. As we approach Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, we repeat: Teshuvah, Tefillah, Tzedakah (תשובה תפלה וצדקה) — repentance, prayer, and righteous giving — ma'avirin et ro'a hagezeirah (מעבירין את רע הגזרה), can sweeten even a harsh decree. The flow of this is like what we have been working on throughout all of Devarim: First we turn inward with teshuvah, a self-reflection to own what I am responsible for and to make that right. Then we speak upward, asking Hashem to help make right between me and others and me and Him. Finally, we act outward with tzedakah, where my physical mitzvot impact those around me in a way where I can help, show, and elevate. Each step strengthens the covenant we all share.

The Answer — Why Am I Responsible?

Because covenant is not a contract with the crowd; it is a marriage between God and each of us, renewed in every generation. Hashem addresses kulchem — "all of you" — but also le'ovrecha (לעברך) — "that you may pass into the covenant" (Deut. 29:11), in the singular. The nation stands as one body, yet every individual is a vital organ. If even one part fails, the whole is diminished. My responsibility is not a burden but a calling: to be the well-digger, the light-bearer, the person whose private faith and public action invite blessing to the entire community.

Atem nitzavim hayom kulchem — we stand today, all of us, together. And because we stand together, my choices matter. My growth protects others, my prayer lifts others, my tzedakah sustains others. I am responsible because I am indispensable.

Reflection Questions

How am I contributing to my community? Or am I living as though I'm disconnected?

What "silent tochachah" am I modeling through my behavior in public?

Where can I act today to help lift someone else?

ROSH HASHANAH — The Ladder of Return

Rosh Hashanah marks not only the beginning of a new year but the renewal of our very selves. It is the coronation of Hashem as King, yet at the same time, it is profoundly personal. The shofar's cry awakens what words cannot reach — the soul's raw yearning to come home.

Rosh Hashanah is the day we recall creation — Hayom harat olam (היום הרת עולם) — "Today the world was born." But it's also the birthday of our awareness. We step back and ask: what kind of world am I creating this year through my choices, words, and inner life?

Teshuvah — Returning to the Core

The Rambam (Hilchot Teshuvah 2:2) defines teshuvah as the moment one says, "I am no longer the person who did this." True return is not only about regret; it's about renewal — choosing to become the person Hashem always intended. The shofar's blasts — Tekiah, Shevarim, Teruah — mirror that process: clarity, brokenness, and repair. We begin whole, become fragmented, and then cry out for restoration.

The Midrash compares the shofar to the cry of a child. A parent may hear many voices, but when their own child cries, they rush instantly to comfort. So too with Hashem — the shofar breaks through the heavens not through eloquence, but through sincerity.

Coronation and Connection

We call Rosh Hashanah Yom HaZikaron — the Day of Remembrance — yet Hashem never forgets. What is remembered is not facts but relationships. Each of us is recalled before the King not as a statistic but as a beloved soul. The Machzor repeatedly says, "Zochreinu l'chaim" (זכרנו לחיים) — "Remember us for life." But Chazal teach that life here means connection — "for in You is the fountain of life" (כי עמך מקור חיים) (Tehillim 36:10). To be remembered by Hashem is to be reconnected to the Source of all being.

A Ladder Between Heaven and Earth

The Zohar describes Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur as two ends of a ladder. Rosh Hashanah is the base — the beginning of ascent, the moment we commit to climb. Yom Kippur is the top — when the light of atonement completes our return. The days between them, the Aseret Yemei Teshuvah, are the rungs. Each tefillah, each small act of kindness, each word of forgiveness lifts us higher.

Sweetness in Judgment

The Simanim — apples in honey, round challot, pomegranates — remind us that judgment and sweetness can coexist. Hashem's din is not meant to destroy but to refine. The Malbim writes that just as honey transforms bitterness into delight, so too teshuvah transforms justice into mercy. When we approach Rosh Hashanah with awe, we discover joy; when we face accountability, we find love.

Standing Before the King

The heart of Rosh Hashanah is Malchuyot — proclaiming Hashem's Kingship. The Baal Shem Tov explains that when a king enters the city, the people go out to greet him with song. Rosh Hashanah is that moment — we leave our comfort zones to meet the King in the field. The awe we feel is not fear of punishment, but reverence for being seen and chosen. Hashem's Kingship is not distant majesty; it's closeness made holy.

As we stand before Hashem this Rosh Hashanah, may the shofar's sound open our hearts to listen, our minds to remember, and our souls to return. May we be written and sealed for a year of growth, clarity, and sweetness.

Reflection Questions

What kind of world am I creating through my choices this year?

If I could say "I am no longer the person who did this," what would that be?

How can I prepare to hear the shofar not just with my ears, but with my heart?

L'shanah tovah tikateivu v'teichateimu.

PARASHAT VAYELECH — Living Beyond the Self

In Parashat Vayelech, Moshe Rabbeinu prepares to take leave of this world. The Torah tells us, "Vayelech Moshe" (וילך משה) — and Moshe went." (Devarim 31:1) But where was he going? Chazal ask this question because the Torah doesn't say explicitly. Some explain that Moshe was going to the tents of Israel to say goodbye personally to each shevet, to each family. Others explain that he went simply to walk — to continue doing, even at the end, because a true leader never stops giving of himself.

Moshe says, "I am one hundred and twenty years old today; I can no longer go out and come in." (בן מאה ועשרים שנה אנכי היום לא אוכל עוד לצאת ולבוא) (31:2) Yet it wasn't that Moshe had lost physical strength — the Torah later says explicitly that his vigor had not diminished. Rather, it means his role was changing. Hashem had told him, "You shall not cross the Jordan." His mission as the leader in this world was ending, but his legacy was only beginning.

This transition — from doing to being, from leading to leaving — is one of the deepest lessons of the Torah. It teaches us that living beyond the self means recognizing that what we build through others endures longer than anything we can do alone.

Passing the Torch

Moshe calls Yehoshua and strengthens him before all Israel: "Chazak ve'ematz" (חזק ואמץ) — be strong and courageous, for you shall come with this people into the land" (31:7). Notice the wording — "you shall come with this people," not "you shall bring this people." Rashi comments that Hashem later rephrases it to Yehoshua as "you shall bring," but Moshe first uses gentler language — you will go together with them. It's a subtle act of humility and wisdom. Leadership is not domination; it's guidance. Moshe models the art of empowering another, showing that a true teacher's greatness is measured by the students who surpass him.

Writing Down the Torah

Moshe completes the writing of the Torah and commands that it be placed beside the Aron. This moment marks not only the end of Moshe's prophecy but also the transformation of Torah from oral experience to enduring text. It becomes the eternal covenant between Hashem and Israel — one that would outlast even Moshe himself. In this, Moshe demonstrates that holiness must become tangible, that inspiration must be written down and transmitted, or it risks fading away.

The Courage to Let Go

Moshe's final acts are not of conquest but of surrender. He gives over leadership, gives over Torah, and gives over his own legacy into the hands of others. And in doing so, he teaches us the secret of eternal influence — that when life is lived entirely for Hashem and for others, even death cannot end that life. The Midrash teaches that Moshe's soul left him with a kiss from Hashem — not a tearing away, but a reunion. His humility, his total alignment with Hashem's will, made his departure as peaceful as his mission was profound.

Living Beyond the Self

Each of us faces moments when we must pass something on — our work, our teachings, our love, our example. Vayelech reminds us that greatness lies not in control but in continuity. The true measure of our lives is what remains after us — the Torah, kindness, and faith we've planted in others.

In a world obsessed with recognition, Vayelech whispers a quieter truth: what we do l'shem shamayim never ends. When we live beyond self, our name becomes eternal, not because it's written in history, but because it's inscribed in the hearts of those we've uplifted.

Reflection Questions

What am I holding onto that I need to pass on to others?

How can I empower someone else rather than trying to control them?

What legacy will remain after me—in the hearts of those I've touched?

YOM KIPPUR — The Ladder of Teshuvah and the Joy of Simcha

Yom Kippur is unlike any other day in the Jewish year. It is a day of both awe and intimacy, of silence and song. We call it Yom HaKippurim — a plural form that hints, as the Zohar notes, to both the forgiveness of the day and its resemblance to Purim — a day of joy through revelation.

Throughout Yom Kippur, we repeat Vidui — confession — ten times. Each repetition corresponds to one of the ten sefirot, ten layers of divine connection. Unlike other Yamim Tovim, which have three daily tefillot plus Musaf, Yom Kippur has five: Ma'ariv, Shacharit, Musaf, Mincha, and Ne'ilah — paralleling the five levels of the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah. As we ascend through the prayers, we peel away the layers of concealment until only the pure core remains.

Vidui — Confession and Connection

When we say "Ashamnu, Bagadnu," (אשמנו בגדנו) we are not listing crimes; we are naming distance. Each word acknowledges a place where we turned away. And in naming it, we begin to return. Rambam (Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1) writes that the essence of teshuvah is verbal confession — because speech bridges the gap between inner resolve and outer reality. When I articulate what went wrong, I transform thought into action, regret into renewal.

The Dual Nature of Yom Kippur

On the one hand, Yom Kippur is Yom HaDin — the day of judgment; on the other, it is the happiest day of the year. The Gemara (Taanit 26b) says: "There were no days as joyous for Israel as the Fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur." (לא היו ימים טובים לישראל כחמשה עשר באב וכיום הכפורים) Why joy? Because on this day, we become transparent again — there is nothing left to hide. The barriers that separate us from Hashem fall away, and we rediscover the simplicity of being loved.

White Garments and Wholeness

We wear white on Yom Kippur to resemble the angels, but also to reflect purity in potential. White is not the absence of color; it is the harmony of all colors in balance. So too Yom Kippur is not the absence of life's complexity; it is its full alignment under the light of Hashem. The Kohen Gadol entered the Kodesh HaKodashim wearing simple white linen, representing humility — the ability to approach Hashem with nothing but sincerity.

The Joy of Ne'ilah

The final tefillah, Ne'ilah, is not closure — it is culmination. The gates of heaven are not closing on us; we are closing ourselves in with Hashem. In that final moment, when we cry "Shema Yisrael, Hashem Elokeinu, Hashem Echad," it is not repetition but revelation. We have climbed the ladder from separation to unity. From fear to love. From confession to connection.

After the final Tekiah Gedolah, we do not collapse — we dance. Because teshuvah, when complete, leads to joy. The Rambam (Hilchot Teshuvah 7:6) writes that those who return out of love transform their sins into merits. The very falls that once distanced us now become the steps that lift us higher.

May we merit that our teshuvah this Yom Kippur be not only a cleansing but a rebirth — a return to the simplicity of the soul, where joy and awe, like judgment and mercy, are one.

Reflection Questions

What distance have I created between myself and Hashem this year?

Can I name what I need to confess—not as guilt, but as honest acknowledgment?

What would it feel like to stand before Hashem with nothing left to hide?

PARASHAT HAAZINU — The Song of Listening

As we near the end of the Torah, Parashat Haazinu stands as Moshe Rabbeinu's poetic farewell — a song of both warning and love, rebuke and hope. It is not simply words of prophecy; it is a song because truth, when sung, transcends the limits of intellect and touches the heart.

The parasha opens: "Haazinu hashamayim va'adabeirah, vetishma ha'aretz imrei fi — Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth." (Devarim 32:1) Moshe calls on heaven and earth to serve as witnesses. They are eternal — unlike man — and will always be present to testify that Hashem's covenant endures. But there is also a deeper message here. The heavens represent the spiritual, lofty ideals, while the earth represents the practical, grounded actions. Together they encompass all of life. Haazinu teaches us that the purpose of Torah is to unify both: to make the heavenly audible on earth, to live spirituality in practice.

Listening and Hearing

Moshe uses two different verbs: haazinu (give ear) and tishma (hear). Rashi notes that haazinu refers to listening up close, while tishma suggests hearing from afar. For Moshe, who is close to the heavens, the "listening" is intimate; for the people, rooted in the earth, it is hearing from a distance. Yet both are connected through Torah — the bridge between divine truth and human reality.

Rebuke and Compassion

The song recounts Israel's journey: Hashem's kindness, Israel's rebellion, and Hashem's enduring mercy. "He found them in a desert land… He encircled them, cared for them, guarded them like the pupil of His eye" (ימצאהו בארץ מדבר... יסבבנהו יבוננהו יצרנהו כאישון עינו) (32:10). Even when the people stray, Hashem's protection never fully departs. The rebuke of Haazinu is not meant to crush but to awaken. It is the song of a parent whose love is fierce and eternal, whose disappointment stems from longing, not rejection.

Avodah Zarah Revisited

The recurring theme of Sefer Devarim — the danger of avodah zarah — appears here again, but in musical form. "They provoked Me with alien gods; with abominations they angered Me" (יקנאני בלא אל כעסוני בהבליהם) (32:16). On the surface, these are the sins of idolatry, but spiritually, they represent misplaced trust — in wealth, in power, in self. Moshe's song reveals the root of all avodah zarah: forgetting gratitude, forgetting dependence, forgetting that all sustenance flows from Hashem. The moment we say, "My strength made this," the song falters.

The Balance of Justice and Mercy

"See now that I, I am He, and there is no god with Me; I kill and I give life, I wound and I heal" (ראו עתה כי אני אני הוא ואין אלהים עמדי אני אמית ואחיה מחצתי ואני ארפא) (32:39). The Sifrei explains: Hashem is not two forces — one for good and one for evil — but One. Both judgment and compassion emanate from the same Source. This is the Torah's ultimate message against dualism. Every event in life, sweet or bitter, is part of one divine harmony.

Haazinu as Personal Reflection

Each of us has our own Haazinu — our personal song, the story of where we've seen Hashem's kindness, where we've fallen, and how we've returned. Moshe's song is not only about the nation; it's about the individual journey from distance to closeness, from pride to humility, from self to surrender.

Hearing as Believing

When Bnei Yisrael accepted the Torah, they said, "Na'aseh v'nishma" (נעשה ונשמע) — "We will do, and we will hear." In Haazinu, Moshe echoes that same ideal. Real faith is not blind doing nor detached understanding; it is the harmony of both. Hearing leads to action, and action deepens hearing. It is the cycle of teshuvah itself.

As Moshe's words conclude, he reminds the people that Torah is not just lofty wisdom: "For it is not an empty thing for you, for it is your life" (כי לא דבר רק הוא מכם כי הוא חייכם) (32:47). Torah is the song of existence — it animates every breath, every moment. To forget it is to lose the melody of life itself.

Reflection Questions

What is my personal "song"—where have I seen Hashem's kindness and where have I fallen?

Am I listening closely (haazinu) or only hearing from afar (tishma)?

Can I see both the sweet and bitter events of my life as part of one divine harmony?

SUKKOT — The Makom Kadosh of Bitul and Equality

We have made it through the first half of Chodesh Tishrei — through Rosh Hashanah, Aseret Yemei Teshuvah, and Yom Kippur. Before that came Elul, and before that Av — months of introspection, accounting, and renewal. Each period brought its own reckoning: Who am I? Where am I? What is my value within Klal Yisrael? We have spent weeks confronting ourselves, striving to peel away layers of ego and error, to return fully through teshuvah sheleimah.

And now, after all of that awe and seriousness, Hashem gives us something that seems almost surprising: to go outside, live in a hut for seven days, and shake together four species of plants. After such intensity, it feels almost whimsical — but in truth, it is profoundly deep.

From Awe to Bitul

A friend once expressed it beautifully: when we all sit in the sukkah, we enter a space of bitul, of dissolving the self. The sukkah is a makom kadosh, a holy space, not because of grandeur but because of simplicity. We leave our homes — symbols of permanence and ego — and dwell in fragility. The schach lets in sunlight and starlight, reminding us that what shelters us is not our craftsmanship but Hashem's presence.

Unity and Equality

The sukkah is the great equalizer. The wealthy man and the pauper, the scholar and the simple Jew — all sit under the same type of roof. Just as the ananei hakavod surrounded all Israel equally, so too the sukkah embraces every Jew without distinction. In that space, we return to the pure awareness that our worth comes not from possessions or status, but from being creations of Hashem.

The Arba Minim — A Symbol of Oneness

The lulav, etrog, hadas, and aravah represent different kinds of Jews: those with Torah and good deeds, those with one or neither. But the mitzvah is only fulfilled when they are bound together. No single species can complete the mitzvah alone. The message is clear: holiness is collective. Klal Yisrael's beauty is in its diversity unified under Hashem.

Joy After Atonement

After Yom Kippur's cleansing comes Sukkot's joy — Zman Simchateinu. Joy is the natural state of a soul aligned with truth. Having stripped away the layers of ego through teshuvah, we can now celebrate simplicity: life itself, air, light, community, Torah.

The Simplicity of Joy — Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot

I was walking home from a friend's sukkah, and as I wished a neighbor a Chag Sameach, he replied in kind — then asked me a great question: "Why is Sukkot called the time of our joy?" The Torah commands us to rejoice — "V'samachta b'chagecha" — but why now, after such awe and fasting? The answer lies in the essence of the water libation — the Nisuch HaMayim. Unlike the wine offering, which symbolizes complexity and struggle, water is simple, essential, life-giving, and accessible to all. That is why the Simchat Beit HaSho'eva — the water-drawing celebration — was the most joyous event in the Temple. Water represents Torah itself — "Ein mayim ela Torah."

The Cost of Water and the Cost of Torah

Water costs nothing yet sustains everything. It falls from heaven, filling all crevices equally. Torah, too, flows freely for anyone who humbles himself to receive it. Those who seek it with simplicity — without pretense or intellectual arrogance — are filled with life. In the days of the Beit HaMikdash, the water drawing was a prayer for rain, but also a symbol of this truth: we draw down blessing only through humility.

Torah and Water in Daily Life

The joy of Torah is not found only in deep, mystical analysis but also in the simple pshat — the clear water that quenches daily thirst. Like drinking from a spring, we can flavor it with layers of remez, drash, and sod, but the foundation is always the pure source. If I lose the simplicity of Torah, I lose its life-giving essence.

Sukkot reminds us that joy and holiness are not distant ideals. They are found in gratitude, simplicity, and unity. The sukkah teaches us to let go of control; the water teaches us to let go of ego. Together they draw us back to the core of emunah — that Hashem provides, sustains, and loves us.

May the joy of Sukkot flow into our year ahead, refreshing our souls like living water, and may our homes, hearts, and sukkot all become makom kadosh — spaces of holiness and joy.

Reflection Questions

What "permanent dwelling" do I need to step out of to remember what truly shelters me?

Who in my community represents a different "species"—and how can I bind together with them?

How can I embrace simplicity and let go of ego this week?

CONCLUSION

From the opening words of Devarim to the final celebrations of Sukkot, we have traveled a complete journey of the soul. We began with memory and responsibility, confronted our inner idolatries, learned to value the small and the overlooked, opened our eyes to blessing, established boundaries and structure, created practical checklists for living, returned home with gratitude, stood together in covenant, and finally — after the awe of the Yamim Nora'im — celebrated the joy that comes from complete alignment with Hashem's will.

This is not merely a journey through the calendar. It is the map of teshuvah itself: from self-awareness to self-transcendence, from ego to emunah, from isolation to unity, from complexity to simplicity.

Living These Teachings

How do we carry this journey forward into our daily lives? Here are some practical ways to integrate what we've learned:

From Devarim - Memory as Inheritance

Keep a journal of your spiritual journey. What patterns repeat? What have you learned?

Share your family's stories with the next generation — the struggles and the victories

Don't sanitize your past; learn from it honestly

From Va'etchanan - Climbing the Ladder

When you feel jealousy or anger, pause and ask: "What am I placing between myself and Hashem?"

Practice saying Shema with intention, expanding the word "Echad" to feel Hashem's unity in all directions

Work backwards from your highest aspirations: what small step can you take today?

From Eikev - Noticing the Small

Choose one "small" mitzvah you've been overlooking and bring it into consciousness

Practice awareness in mundane moments: tying your shoes, drinking water, opening a door

Value the "small" people in your life — who have you been stepping over?

From Re'eh - Seeing Blessing

Practice reframing: when something appears as a "curse," ask what hidden blessing it might contain

Give tzedakah regularly, even small amounts, to remember that everything comes from Hashem

Keep a gratitude list of specific, personal gifts from Hashem

From Shoftim - Structure and Holiness

Create boundaries in your life that protect kedushah (a ma'akeh for your "roof")

Examine your leadership: are you empowering others or controlling them?

Find ways to bring holiness into the ordinary structures of your day

From Ki Tetzei - The Daily Checklist

Review your derech eretz: how do you treat family, neighbors, employees, strangers?

Practice compassion even toward those you don't like (hashavat aveidah, prikah u'te'ina)

Build healthy boundaries in your relationships and home

From Ki Tavo - Returning with Gratitude

Offer your "first fruits" — the best of your time, energy, and resources — to Hashem

Remove doubt (safek) by resolving conflicts and seeking clarity

Express specific, personal gratitude regularly

From Nitzavim - Standing Responsible

Remember: your choices affect the whole community — act accordingly

Practice "silent tochachah" by living with integrity

Ask yourself: what can I do today that will help lift someone else?

From the Yamim Nora'im - Renewal and Joy

Don't wait for Rosh Hashanah to begin again — every day offers a chance to return

Practice confession (vidui) not as guilt but as honest acknowledgment

After working on yourself, celebrate — joy is the sign of true alignment

From Sukkot - Simplicity and Unity

Regularly step outside your "permanent dwelling" — physically or metaphorically — to remember what really shelters you

Seek out the "four species" in your community — people different from you who complete the picture

Draw down blessing through humility, like water from a spring

A Final Reflection

As we complete this cycle and prepare to begin again with Bereishit, we carry forward everything we have learned. We have seen that holiness is not escape from the world but full presence within it. We have learned that the small matters as much as the great, that giving breaks the chains of idolatry, that responsibility is love made tangible, and that joy is the natural state of a soul aligned with truth.

May we merit to live these lessons throughout the coming year — to see Hashem's hand in every moment, to give generously, to act with integrity, to embrace our responsibilities with joy, and to transform every aspect of our lives into vessels for kedushah.

From self to surrender. From Devarim to Simchat Torah. From year to year, growing closer to the Source of all blessings.
